parts.title: Sentence comprehension: Studio note
parts.instructions: Read the short email from a friend. Choose the best word for each gap (1-5).
parts.passage:
Hi Lara,

I thought I would let you know how my new Saturday pottery course is going. Although I was a bit nervous at first, I soon got [1] to shaping wet clay on the wheel. Our instructor, Rosa, always encourages us to [2] our time instead of rushing each piece. Next weekend we are planning to try a simple glazing technique, [3] I have never done before. You do not need to buy any equipment in advance because the studio [4] all the clay and aprons. Let me know if you are interested in signing [5] for the next beginner group!

Best,
Sam

questions.explanation: 'Get used to + -ing' means becoming comfortable with a new activity; 'familiar' uses 'with' and 'known' does not fit.
'Take our time' is a fixed collocation meaning to work calmly without hurrying.
'Which' introduces a non-defining relative clause referring back to 'a simple glazing technique'.
'Provides all the clay and aprons' means supplies them for students; 'allows' and 'presents' do not fit this meaning.
'Sign up for' is the phrasal verb meaning to register for a course or group.

parts.title: Text cohesion: First ceramic mug
parts.instructions: The first sentence of the text is in the right place. Put the five sentences (A-E) into the correct order (gaps 1-5) to make a clear story.
parts.passage: Last Saturday morning, I arrived at the community studio early to make my very first ceramic mug. [1] [2] [3] [4] [5]
sentences: When I was happy with the shape, I carefully cut the mug off the wheel with a thin wire and set it on a wooden shelf to dry.
Once the clay felt soft and smooth, I placed it in the centre of the spinning wheel and wet my hands.
The teacher explained that it would stay there for a week before going into the hot kiln for its first firing.
First, the teacher handed each of us a cold block of grey clay and showed us how to press out the air bubbles.
At first the lump kept slipping sideways, but after ten minutes of slow practice it finally rose into a small cylinder.

gaps.explanation: 'First, the teacher handed each of us a cold block of grey clay...' begins the step-by-step process immediately after arriving at the studio.
'Once the clay felt soft and smooth' links directly to pressing the cold block of clay in the previous sentence and introduces the spinning wheel.
'At first the lump kept slipping sideways...' describes what happened right after putting the clay on the spinning wheel and ends with forming a small cylinder.
'When I was happy with the shape' refers back to the small cylinder, and 'set it on a wooden shelf to dry' leads into the final sentence.
'It would stay there for a week' refers back to the wooden shelf mentioned in the previous sentence and closes the process with the kiln firing.

parts.title: Opinion matching: Handmade tableware
parts.instructions: Four people (A-D) give their opinions about handmade pottery and everyday tableware. Match each statement (1-7) to the correct person. You can use each person more than once.

texts.title: Nadia
texts.text: I love visiting weekend craft markets because you can chat with the person who actually shaped your mug. Handmade pieces certainly cost more than supermarket ones, so I only buy one or two each year, usually as birthday presents for close friends. For my own kitchen, I avoid very thin porcelain because it chips too easily in the sink. Instead, I look for thick, heavy stoneware that can go safely into the dishwasher every evening.

texts.title: Owen
texts.text: In the café where I work, we use plain factory-made cups because they stack neatly on the counter and cost very little to replace when someone drops one. Buying hand-thrown mugs for a busy business just would not be practical. At home, though, my cupboards are full of hand-painted bowls that I have collected from local potters. None of them match, and I really enjoy noticing the tiny differences in glaze and shape.

texts.title: Priya
texts.text: For years I thought handmade ceramics were far too expensive, and I always ordered cheap sets online. That completely changed after I took an evening pottery class and realised how many hours of work go into a single bowl. Now I happily save up for one well-made plate at a time. My only complaint is that some small craft stalls forget to include clear notes about whether their glazes are safe to put in the microwave.

texts.title: Ruben
texts.text: I run a small gift shop that stocks work from twelve local potters, and I have noticed a big shift in what shoppers ask for. Younger customers rarely want a twelve-piece matching dinner set anymore; they prefer individual bowls with a story behind them. In my view, buying handmade tableware is also better for the planet because people value it more, take care of it, and even repair a cracked dish rather than throwing it away.

parts.title: Long text comprehension: Everyday pottery
parts.instructions: Read the article about the history and modern revival of everyday pottery. Match each paragraph (1-7) to the best heading (A-H). There is one extra heading that you do not need.

paragraphs.text: Long before humans learned to work with metal, they discovered that wet river mud became hard and waterproof when baked in a hot fire. Early pots were built by rolling clay into long ropes and stacking them in circles, then smoothing the walls with a flat stone or a shell. These simple vessels changed daily life completely. For the first time, families could boil grains, store dried seeds away from hungry insects, and carry clean water over long distances without spilling it along the way.

Around five thousand years ago, craftspeople in ancient cities began using a flat turntable spun by hand or foot. This early potter's wheel allowed a skilled worker to pull up a tall, even jar in minutes rather than hours. Because pots could now be produced much faster and in regular sizes, pottery stopped being just a household chore done beside the cooking fire. Dedicated workshops appeared near clay beds and rivers, and skilled potters started trading their bowls and jugs across neighbouring towns.

Plain baked clay is strong, yet water still slowly leaks through tiny holes in its surface. To solve this problem, ancient makers experimented with natural minerals, wood ash, and crushed sand that melted into a shiny glass coat inside the kiln. Not only did these glazes seal jars tightly enough to hold oil and wine, they also opened a new world of colour. Deep blues from cobalt, soft greens from copper, and bright reds from iron turned ordinary kitchenware into prized works of art.

When large steam-powered factories opened in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, ceramic production changed at breathtaking speed. Workers poured liquid clay into plaster moulds to make hundreds of identical teacups and dinner plates every single day. Prices fell sharply, so ordinary households could suddenly afford neat, matching tableware that had once belonged only to wealthy families. At the same time, many small village workshops struggled to compete with factory prices and gradually closed their doors.

Beyond the kitchen table, fired clay quietly holds clues to past civilisations that paper and wood can never provide. While cloth rots and iron rusts away in damp soil, broken pieces of pottery survive underground for thousands of years almost unchanged. By studying the shape of a rim, the type of local sand mixed into the clay, or a painted pattern on a shard, historians can trace ancient trade routes, estimate the size of forgotten towns, and even discover what people cooked for dinner.

In the last decade, an unexpected wave of interest in pottery has swept through modern cities. Office workers, students, and retired people alike are signing up for evening studio classes, often waiting months for a free space at the wheel. Many learners say that shaping wet clay forces them to put down their phones and focus completely on a slow, physical task. In a world of instant digital messages, waiting weeks to see a finished mug come out of the kiln feels surprisingly calming.

Today's community studios are also rethinking how ceramics affect the environment. Firing a kiln to over twelve hundred degrees uses a large amount of energy, so many potters now share kiln space to make sure every load is packed completely full. Others collect scrap clay from the studio floor, soak it in buckets, and recycle it into fresh blocks instead of throwing it away. By combining old hand skills with cleaner modern habits, small studios hope to keep the craft thriving for future generations.

headings: A lasting record for studying the past
A new tool turns a home skill into a trade
A slow hobby offers relief from screen life
How modern museums display rare painted vases
Early pots transform how people store and cook food
Cheaper factory methods reshape everyday dining
Melted coatings add both function and beauty

gaps.explanation: Paragraph 1 explains how early baked-clay pots allowed people for the first time to boil grains, store seeds, and carry water.
Paragraph 2 describes how the invention of the potter's wheel sped up production and led to dedicated workshops trading pots between towns.
Paragraph 3 explains how melted mineral glazes both sealed clay jars against leaks (function) and added rich colours (beauty).
Paragraph 4 focuses on how factory moulds lowered prices and brought matching tableware to ordinary homes while squeezing village workshops.
Paragraph 5 explains that broken pottery survives underground for millennia, helping historians study ancient trade routes, towns, and diets.
Paragraph 6 describes why busy city dwellers join pottery classes to step away from phones and enjoy a slow, calming physical task.
Paragraph 7 explains how modern studios reduce environmental impact by sharing full kiln loads and recycling scrap clay.

task.title: Riverside Pottery Club — Schedule and fee update

sourceEmail.subject: Temporary change to evening classes and monthly fee
sourceEmail.body:
Dear Members,

Our main electric kiln needs a repair and will be out of service for four weeks. During this time, we are sharing a smaller kiln with a partner studio, so Tuesday evening classes will move to Thursday evenings from 7:00 to 9:00 pm. In addition, the monthly materials and firing fee will increase by £6 starting next month because of higher electricity prices.

Please contact us if you have any questions or suggestions.

Kind regards,
Helen Foster
Club Manager

2. Formal email to the club manager, Helen Foster (120-150 words): explain your feelings about the moved class and higher fee, and suggest a practical solution for members.

parts.title: Monologue comprehension
parts.instructions: Listen to two speakers giving short talks: first a museum curator about a tile exhibition (questions 1-2), then a ceramic artist about starting her own studio business (questions 3-4). Choose the best answer for each question.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: First, you will hear Martin, a museum curator, talking about a new exhibition of painted ceramic tiles.

turns.speaker: martin
turns.text: When we began planning our exhibition on historical painted tiles, most colleagues assumed we would line them up in strict date order, starting in the sixteenth century and finishing in the twentieth. After all, that's how museums usually work. Yet whenever I watched visitors walk through traditional date-ordered rooms, they quickly grew tired of reading dates and forgot why the objects existed in the first place. So we grouped the tiles by where people actually lived with them: kitchen stoves, courtyard fountains, and bakery walls. That way, visitors immediately see how ordinary families used colour and pattern to brighten practical spaces. I expected architecture students to love the display, and they did. What genuinely caught me off guard, though, was how many older visitors stayed for nearly an hour sketching the geometric borders in notebooks so they could paint similar designs on plant pots at home. Seeing a historical collection spark fresh creative projects felt far more rewarding than any newspaper review.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Now you will hear Evelyn, a ceramic artist, talking about turning her pottery hobby into a full-time business.

turns.speaker: evelyn
turns.text: People often imagine that running a small pottery studio means spending eight peaceful hours a day shaping clay with music playing softly in the background. I certainly pictured that when I left my office job three years ago! In reality, the shaping itself takes up less than half my week. The toughest adjustment for me wasn't the physical tiredness or even the occasional broken kiln load — it was learning to manage invoices, packaging orders safely, and updating my website every evening. Nobody warns you how much desk work hides behind a handmade business. Still, I wouldn't trade it for my old career. Whenever hobby potters ask me if they should quit their jobs and start selling, I tell them not to rush into renting an expensive workshop straight away. Test your designs at two or three weekend markets first, talk directly to customers, and see which pieces genuinely sell before you spend your savings on heavy equipment.

To help visitors understand their daily purpose

questions.explanation: Martin says what genuinely caught him off guard was how many older visitors spent nearly an hour sketching the borders to paint on plant pots at home.
